## [08 · Digital Logic Design](../../courses/08-digital-logic-design/README.md)

### [08-01 · Number Systems and Codes](../../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-01-number-systems-and-codes.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"18 PFLOPS of FP4 per GPU."** *Reality:* NVIDIA's HGX B200 page lists FP4 at "144 PFLOPS | 72 PFLOPS" for eight GPUs, footnoted as sparse and dense, with dense half of sparse: **18** against **9** PFLOPS per GPU ([R-147](../../reference/research-log.md#r-147--accelerator-throughput-specifications)). The sparse figure assumes weights with structured zeros that most models do not have, and launch-event headlines quoted yet another figure (up to 20) **[Contested]** (which configuration each figure refers to). *Sanity check:* ask for dense throughput, in the format your model will actually use, and for sustained utilization on a named workload.
- **"DDR5 has ECC built in."** *Reality:* on-die ECC corrects single-bit errors inside the chip, silently. It cannot flag double errors and never reports to the system. A machine without side-band ECC modules has no end-to-end memory protection. *Sanity check:* ask whether the modules are side-band ECC modules, with extra DRAM chips for check bits, and whether the platform logs corrected errors.
- **"No accuracy loss at 4 bits."** *Reality:* the vendor's own claim is "1% or less" against FP8 on selected benchmarks, with two-level scaling and a calibration recipe. Results vary by model and task. *Sanity check:* ask which models and benchmarks, against which baseline, and whether the model was retrained for the format.
- **"Protected by a CRC."** *Reality:* a CRC detects accidental errors only (anyone can recompute it for altered data), and its guarantees depend on message length: Ethernet's CRC-32 guarantees detection of every error of up to 3 bits at full frame length, not more. *Sanity check:* ask for the Hamming distance at the actual message length and what end-to-end check sits above the link.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"Which number formats does the datapath support natively, and in what precision does it accumulate?"**
   - *Strong:* names element formats, block sizes and scale formats, states the accumulator width (e.g. FP32 accumulation of FP8 products) and the cost of converting between formats.
   - *Evasive:* "we support FP4", with no word on scaling or accumulation.
2. **"What accuracy do models lose going from FP8 to FP4, and with what recipe?"**
   - *Strong:* per-model evaluation tables, the calibration or retraining method, and the cases where FP4 fails.
   - *Evasive:* "negligible", or a single favorable benchmark.
3. **"Is that throughput figure dense or sparse, and at which format?"**
   - *Strong:* dense figures for each format, plus measured utilization on real workloads.
   - *Evasive:* quotes only the sparse peak in the narrowest format.
4. **"What protects memory end to end?"**
   - *Strong:* on-die ECC plus side-band SEC-DED or stronger codes, scrubbing, and error logs reviewed in the field.
   - *Evasive:* "DDR5 has ECC."
5. **"What residual error rate do your links have, and what catches what the link CRC misses?"**
   - *Strong:* a bit-error-rate target, forward error correction where used, the CRC's Hamming distance at the frame length, and an end-to-end checksum in software.
   - *Evasive:* "the link has a CRC."

### [08-02 · Boolean Algebra and Logic Gates](../../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-02-boolean-algebra-and-gates.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"208 billion transistors."** *Reality:* it is two dies in one package, so the per-die count (about 104 billion) is the like-for-like comparison with single-die chips. *Sanity check:* ask for transistors per die, die area, and how much of it is SRAM.
- **"A 10-million-gate design."** *Reality:* gate equivalents are an area unit tied to one library's NAND2, and FPGA vendors have used still other "gate" and "logic cell" units. *Sanity check:* ask which library or device family, and convert to the same unit before comparing.
- **"Open-source PDK, ready for production."** *Reality:* the SKY130 PDK's own repository calls it an experimental preview. Open PDKs are excellent for education and shuttles; production tape-outs depend on foundry support and qualification. *Sanity check:* ask what the foundry warrants and what the design's yield and reliability data are based on.
- **"Our tool optimized the logic, so it's correct."** *Reality:* synthesis transforms are checked by formal equivalence, not trusted. *Sanity check:* ask whether every netlist is equivalence-checked against the RTL, and how waived differences are reviewed.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"How large is the design in gate equivalents, in which library, and how much of the die is logic versus SRAM, I/O and analog?"**
   - *Strong:* gives a GE count with the reference library, and an area breakdown by block type.
   - *Evasive:* quotes only a transistor count.
2. **"How do you know the synthesized netlist matches the RTL?"**
   - *Strong:* formal equivalence checking at every handoff (RTL to gates, gates to placed netlist, after every manual change), with a sign-off rule for waivers.
   - *Evasive:* "we ran the regression tests."
3. **"Which standard-cell libraries do you use, and how many drive strengths and threshold-voltage flavors?"**
   - *Strong:* names the libraries and explains how multi-threshold cells trade leakage against speed in their flow.
   - *Evasive:* "whatever the foundry gives us."
4. **"Where does the chip's power go?"**
   - *Strong:* splits dynamic switching power from leakage, by block, measured or from sign-off analysis.
   - *Evasive:* gives a single TDP figure.

### [08-03 · Logic Minimization: K-Maps and Beyond](../../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-03-logic-minimization.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"Our AI-driven synthesis improves PPA by X%."** *Reality:* power, performance and area gains are design-, node- and constraint-specific, and are usually reported against the vendor's own previous flow. *Sanity check:* ask for results on your designs, at your constraints, with equivalence checking passed and the same sign-off timing.
- **"The EDA market is $X billion."** *Reality:* totals depend on whether semiconductor IP, simulation software from acquisitions such as Ansys, and services are counted; the ESD Alliance's "electronic system design" figure includes IP. *Sanity check:* ask which categories are included before comparing growth rates or shares.
- **"Revenue grew 15%."** *Reality:* Synopsys's FY2025 growth was about 15.1% as reported but about 2.8% without the acquired Ansys revenue (§9 above). Reported growth mixes organic growth with acquisitions. *Sanity check:* ask for organic growth on a like-for-like basis, and which part of the business it came from.
- **"Optimal logic."** *Reality:* exact minimization is intractable for real designs, so every tool is heuristic; "optimal" means "best this tool found within its run time". *Sanity check:* ask how results vary with effort settings and run time.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"How do you measure synthesis quality of results, and against what baseline?"**
   - *Strong:* reports area, timing and power on a fixed benchmark set of their own designs, under fixed constraints, across tool versions.
   - *Evasive:* "the tool's default settings are fine."
2. **"Where does your flow rely on open-source tools, and where on commercial ones?"**
   - *Strong:* gives a clear map (for example open-source for FPGA prototyping and lint, commercial for sign-off) with reasons.
   - *Evasive:* cannot say which tools touch the tape-out database.
3. **"How do you handle don't-care conditions in specifications?"**
   - *Strong:* specifies illegal-state behavior explicitly for safety-relevant logic, and checks it in verification.
   - *Evasive:* "the synthesis tool optimizes them."
4. **"What fraction of your engineering budget goes to EDA licenses, and how does it scale with headcount and tape-outs?"**
   - *Strong:* knows the number and its drivers, and the negotiation calendar.
   - *Evasive:* "procurement handles that."

### [08-04 · Combinational Building Blocks](../../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-04-combinational-building-blocks.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"Propagation delay: 30 ns."** *Reality:* that is a typical value, at one voltage, load and temperature. The guaranteed maximum is about twice as large over temperature, and timing must close against the maximum. *Sanity check:* ask for the max over the full operating range, at your supply voltage and load.
- **"Our ALU does N operations per cycle."** *Reality:* throughput claims assume the operands are ready and the results are consumed; the critical path through the adder and bypass multiplexers sets the cycle time. *Sanity check:* ask what limits the clock period, and what the latency of one dependent operation is.
- **"Glitch-free by design."** *Reality:* a two-level SOP is hazard-free only if it includes the needed consensus terms, and synthesis tools remove them as redundant unless told not to. *Sanity check:* ask how clock, reset and asynchronous outputs are protected (registered outputs, dedicated clock-gating cells, preserved logic).

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"What is the critical path in this block, and how much timing margin does it have at the worst-case corner?"**
   - *Strong:* names the path (for example the carry chain through the adder into the bypass multiplexer) and quotes slack at the slow corner.
   - *Evasive:* "it meets timing at typical."
2. **"Which signals in the design are used without a clock, and how are they kept glitch-free?"**
   - *Strong:* lists resets, clock enables and outputs to asynchronous devices, and says they come straight from flip-flops or from glitch-free library cells.
   - *Evasive:* "everything is synchronous" (it never is).
3. **"How do you verify the ALU and datapath, and against what reference?"**
   - *Strong:* exhaustive or constrained-random comparison against a reference model, formal equivalence for arithmetic blocks, and coverage of flag corner cases (overflow, zero, borrow).
   - *Evasive:* "we ran the compiler test suite."

### [08-05 · Introduction to Verilog/SystemVerilog and Testbenches](../../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-05-verilog-and-testbenches.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"The fastest Verilog/SystemVerilog simulator."** *Reality:* Verilator's README makes this claim and says it is "about 100 times faster than interpreted Verilog simulators" on a single thread **[Industry estimate]** (the project's own claim, benchmark conditions unstated). Compiled two-state simulation is much faster for long cycle-based runs, but it does not model X and Z or detailed event timing. *Sanity check:* ask what was simulated, at what abstraction, with which features turned off, and against which competitor version.
- **"100% code coverage."** *Reality:* every line executed does not mean every behavior checked; a testbench with a weak checker can execute every line and still miss bugs. *Sanity check:* ask about functional coverage of specified scenarios and about the quality of the reference model.
- **"It passed simulation."** *Reality:* simulation with an incomplete sensitivity list, unchecked X values or untested corner cases passes routinely. *Sanity check:* ask whether the RTL is lint-clean, whether the netlist was equivalence-checked against the RTL, and what found the last three bugs.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"How do you know a block is verified?"**
   - *Strong:* a verification plan with functional-coverage targets, reference models, closure reports, and bug-discovery rates trending toward zero.
   - *Evasive:* "the tests pass."
2. **"What runs in CI on every commit?"**
   - *Strong:* lint, unit testbenches, regression subsets, with results visible to the team.
   - *Evasive:* "we run the full regression before tape-out."
3. **"Which simulators and versions do you depend on, and how do you handle differences between them?"**
   - *Strong:* a pinned tool matrix, and code that follows rules (non-blocking for sequential logic, no races) so results do not depend on the simulator.
   - *Evasive:* "we only use vendor X."
4. **"How much of your verification uses formal methods or assertions?"**
   - *Strong:* assertions in interfaces and FSMs, formal proofs for arithmetic and protocol blocks.
   - *Evasive:* "simulation is enough."

### [08-06 · Latches, Flip-Flops and Sequential Timing](../../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-06-latches-and-flip-flops.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"The design runs at X GHz."** *Reality:* at which corner (process, voltage, temperature), with what margin, on which paths? A chip that meets timing at the typical corner may fail at the slow corner and high temperature. *Sanity check:* ask for the sign-off corners and the worst negative slack at each.
- **"Setup time 3 ns."** *Reality:* datasheet setup and hold are guaranteed limits under stated conditions; ignoring the supply voltage, temperature and load columns, or the minimum delays needed for hold, is a classic board-design error. *Sanity check:* recompute both constraints with worst-case values from the datasheet.
- **"No hold issues in our design."** *Reality:* hold depends on clock skew, which is only known after the clock tree is built; early claims mean little. *Sanity check:* ask whether hold was checked after clock-tree synthesis, at the fast corner, and how many hold buffers were inserted.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"What sets your clock frequency: logic depth, flip-flop overhead, or wires?"**
   - *Strong:* names the critical paths, the share of each cycle spent in registers and in wire delay, and what the next pipeline change would buy.
   - *Evasive:* "the process is fast enough."
2. **"How do you handle resets?"**
   - *Strong:* asynchronous assertion, synchronous release through reset synchronizers per clock domain, and a list of which registers need reset at all.
   - *Evasive:* "everything is reset asynchronously."
3. **"At which corners did you sign off setup and hold, and how many hold-fix buffers did you add?"**
   - *Strong:* gives the corner list (slow corner for setup, fast for hold, with on-chip variation margins) and a buffer count with its area and power cost.
   - *Evasive:* "the tool fixed everything."
4. **"How much of your dynamic power is in the clock network and flip-flops?"**
   - *Strong:* a measured or estimated split, and the clock-gating coverage.
   - *Evasive:* no breakdown.

### [08-07 · Registers, Counters and Shift Registers](../../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-07-registers-counters-shift-registers.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"Error-free with PRBS31 for X hours."** *Reality:* the meaningful number is the bit-error-rate bound that observation supports: with zero errors in $N$ bits, the 95% upper bound is about $3/N$ (the "rule of three" of [03-05](../../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md)). *Sanity check:* convert hours and bit rate into bits, and ask whether the pattern, temperature and channel were worst case.
- **"PRBS31 tests all bit patterns."** *Reality:* every 31-bit pattern but one (all zeros, or all ones in the inverted form) appears exactly once per period, but real traffic with long runs or specific spectra (scrambled or encoded data) can stress a receiver differently. *Sanity check:* ask which patterns were used and why.
- **"Our counter design is glitch-free."** *Reality:* only if outputs are registered or Gray coded; decoded binary or ripple counter outputs glitch. *Sanity check:* ask how counter outputs that leave the clock domain are encoded.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"How do you measure the bit-error rate of your links, and to what confidence?"**
   - *Strong:* PRBS patterns per the standard, BER targets with statistical confidence bounds, worst-case channels and temperatures.
   - *Evasive:* "no errors in the lab."
2. **"Which counters in the design cross clock domains or drive asynchronous logic, and how are they encoded?"**
   - *Strong:* Gray-coded pointers and registered outputs, verified by CDC tools.
   - *Evasive:* "everything is synchronous."
3. **"How do your state machines and counters recover from unused states?"**
   - *Strong:* resets and self-correcting next-state logic, checked in simulation by forcing illegal states.
   - *Evasive:* "they cannot get there."

### [08-08 · Finite State Machines](../../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-08-finite-state-machines.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"100% state coverage."** *Reality:* visiting every state is easy; the bugs live in transitions and sequences. *Sanity check:* ask for transition coverage, and whether illegal-state recovery was tested by forcing bad codes.
- **"Our controller is formally verified."** *Reality:* formal tools prove the specific properties someone wrote, within bounds that may be limited; a property that was never written is never checked. *Sanity check:* ask which properties were proved, whether the proofs were complete or bounded, and how deep.
- **"The FSM cannot hang."** *Reality:* only if every illegal code leads back to a legal state in the *synthesized* encoding, and every wait has a timeout. *Sanity check:* ask what happens after a single-event upset in the state register, and whether every waiting state has a timeout or an exit.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"How do you measure verification completeness on your control logic?"**
   - *Strong:* state and transition coverage, assertions on protocol rules, formal checks on key controllers, illegal-state injection.
   - *Evasive:* "we run a lot of tests."
2. **"What happens if a state register takes a bit flip in the field?"**
   - *Strong:* safe encodings or recovery logic chosen per block criticality, with diagnostic coverage numbers for safety parts.
   - *Evasive:* "the reset fixes it."
3. **"Which of your interface state machines come from a specification, and how do you test compliance?"**
   - *Strong:* the specification's state machines implemented and named as written, compliance suites, interoperability testing with many partners.
   - *Evasive:* "it works with our reference platform."

### [08-09 · Arithmetic Circuits](../../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-09-arithmetic-circuits.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"X PFLOPS."** *Reality:* the number depends on the format (FP4 against FP8 halves or doubles it), on sparsity (structured sparsity doubles it again on paper) and on whether it is per chip or per system. *Sanity check:* ask for dense throughput at the format your model actually runs, and what accumulator precision is used.
- **"INT8 is as accurate as FP32."** *Reality:* for many inference workloads, after careful calibration and sometimes retraining; not automatically, and not for every layer. *Sanity check:* ask which layers stay in higher precision and what the measured accuracy loss is.
- **"Our MAC array is 95% utilized."** *Reality:* peak arithmetic is cheap; feeding it is expensive (a cache read costs far more than the MAC). *Sanity check:* ask for utilization on real models at batch sizes customers use.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"Which number formats does the datapath support natively, and with what accumulator widths?"**
   - *Strong:* a list with accumulator precision, rounding modes and how scaling factors are handled.
   - *Evasive:* "we support all the formats."
2. **"What limits your clock frequency, and is it arithmetic or wiring?"**
   - *Strong:* the critical paths named, with how adder architecture and floorplan were traded.
   - *Evasive:* "the foundry process."
3. **"How do you verify your arithmetic units?"**
   - *Strong:* exhaustive tests for small units, formal equivalence against reference models, and random plus corner-case testing for wide ones.
   - *Evasive:* "we ran a lot of vectors."
4. **"What happens on overflow in your fixed-point paths?"**
   - *Strong:* saturation at defined points, guard-bit analysis, and tests that drive extreme inputs.
   - *Evasive:* "it does not overflow in practice."

### [08-10 · Timing, Metastability and Clock-Domain Crossing](../../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-10-timing-metastability-cdc.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"MTBF of a billion years."** *Reality:* usually per synchronizer, at nominal conditions. A chip has hundreds to thousands of crossings and a product ships millions of units, so fleet failure rates are the sum (Problem 08-10.13). *Sanity check:* ask for the MTBF at the worst voltage and temperature, per chip, multiplied by the installed base.
- **"Our design is fully synchronous."** *Reality:* almost no SoC is; external interfaces, power-management clocks and debug logic cross domains. *Sanity check:* ask how many clock domains there are and how the crossings are verified.
- **"Timing is closed at 3 GHz."** *Reality:* at which corners, with what margin, and with which paths declared false or multicycle? *Sanity check:* ask for the worst-corner frequency and how timing exceptions were reviewed.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"How do you verify clock-domain crossings, and how many waivers does the CDC report carry?"**
   - *Strong:* structural CDC sign-off on every crossing, with waivers reviewed individually and few in number.
   - *Evasive:* "simulation covers it."
2. **"What is the system-level synchronizer MTBF, at the worst corner, across your installed base?"**
   - *Strong:* a number, with the assumptions (τ at low voltage, number of crossings, fleet size).
   - *Evasive:* "two flip-flops everywhere."
3. **"Which timing exceptions (false and multicycle paths) do you have, and who approves them?"**
   - *Strong:* a reviewed list with owners, checked by formal or simulation methods.
   - *Evasive:* "the tool handles it."
4. **"How much margin do you hold for on-chip variation, aging and jitter at sign-off?"**
   - *Strong:* specific margins per corner, correlated with silicon measurements.
   - *Evasive:* "standard foundry margins."

### [08-11 · Memories and Programmable Logic](../../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-11-memories-and-programmable-logic.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"10 million logic cells."** *Reality:* "system logic cells" are a vendor-defined scaled count; the LUT count is lower (4.09 million LUTs for the VU19P's 8.9 million logic cells). *Sanity check:* compare LUTs, flip-flops, block RAM bits and DSP blocks, and how many can be used at once while still meeting timing.
- **"Runs at 500 MHz."** *Reality:* hard blocks may run that fast; a full design with routing usually runs much slower. *Sanity check:* ask for the achieved frequency of a comparable design, not the block's datasheet maximum.
- **"The FPGA market will grow at X% a year."** *Reality:* forecasts disagree by tens of percent on the base year alone (§9). *Sanity check:* reconcile any top-down estimate with the vendors' reported revenues.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"What fraction of your die is memory, and how did you choose its organization?"**
   - *Strong:* a breakdown by memory type, with the compiler or custom design choices and their power.
   - *Evasive:* "we use the foundry's memory compiler."
2. **"How many register-file ports does your core have, and how did you contain their cost?"**
   - *Strong:* port counts, clustering or banking choices, and the timing impact.
   - *Evasive:* "standard design."
3. **"Why FPGA rather than ASIC (or the reverse) for this product, at what volume does that flip, and what is the plan if it does?"**
   - *Strong:* a break-even analysis including NRE, unit cost, power and time to market, with a migration path.
   - *Evasive:* "flexibility."
4. **"How do you prototype your next chip before tape-out?"**
   - *Strong:* FPGA prototyping or emulation capacity, how much of the design it covers, and how early software runs on it.
   - *Evasive:* "simulation."

### [08-12 · FPGA Implementation Flow](../../courses/08-digital-logic-design/chapters/08-12-fpga-implementation-flow.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"The DSP block runs at X MHz."** *Reality:* a full design including routing between blocks runs slower; in the lab, routing was two thirds of the DSP multiplier harness's critical path. *Sanity check:* ask for the achieved frequency of a complete, comparable design.
- **"Open-source tools match vendor tools."** *Reality:* for some families they work well end to end; for large devices they are experimental or missing. *Sanity check:* ask which device family and which results were compared.
- **"95% utilization, timing met."** *Reality:* possible, but usually after heavy floorplanning and many iterations; congestion rises sharply at high utilization. *Sanity check:* ask how much headroom is planned for later features.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"How long does a full FPGA or ASIC build take, and how often do you run it?"**
   - *Strong:* build times, nightly or per-change builds in CI, and tracked timing trends.
   - *Evasive:* "when we need to."
2. **"How are your timing constraints written and reviewed?"**
   - *Strong:* constraints under version control, reviewed like RTL, with exceptions justified individually.
   - *Evasive:* "the tool generates them."
3. **"Which hard blocks does the design rely on, and what happens if you change device family?"**
   - *Strong:* an inventory of DSP, memory and transceiver use, with portable RTL and wrappers.
   - *Evasive:* "we won't change."
4. **"What is your utilization and timing margin today, and what is planned for future features?"**
   - *Strong:* specific numbers and a plan (bigger device, pipelining) if features grow.
   - *Evasive:* "it fits."

## [14 · Computer Organization and Architecture](../../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/README.md)

### [14-01 · Performance, Power and the Iron Law](../../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-01-performance-power-iron-law.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"Up to 2× performance."** *Reality:* "up to" is the best case, usually one benchmark or kernel. *Sanity check:* ask for the geometric mean across a named suite and for the workload you run, at the same power.
- **"40% better performance per watt."** *Reality:* efficiency depends on the operating point; a new chip measured at a lower point on its voltage curve than the old one gains "efficiency" without any architectural improvement. *Sanity check:* ask for the full performance-against-power curve of both chips, or compare at equal performance and at equal power.
- **"Linear scaling to 1,000 cores."** *Reality:* usually weak (Gustafson) scaling with the problem grown in proportion. *Sanity check:* ask for strong scaling (fixed problem) and the serial fraction it implies.
- **"N TOPS."** *Reality:* a peak rate of operations at a stated precision, often with sparsity counted as work done (14-15). *Sanity check:* ask for delivered throughput on a named model, at a stated precision and batch size.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"On which workloads, at what power, did you measure the speedup?"**
   *Strong:* a named suite and named customer workloads, run at equal power and at equal performance, with the geometric mean and the per-benchmark spread. *Evasive:* "up to" a single number on one kernel.
2. **"Where does the time go?"**
   *Strong:* a measured breakdown (compute, memory stalls, branch mispredictions, synchronization) that justifies what the new design changed. *Evasive:* the improvement is described only by peak rates.
3. **"What fraction of your target applications is serial, and what does that cap your speedup at?"**
   *Strong:* profiled serial fractions and the Amdahl ceiling, with strong-scaling curves. *Evasive:* weak-scaling results only.
4. **"How much of your power is leakage, and how do you manage idle?"**
   *Strong:* the dynamic/static split at typical operating points, power-gating granularity and wake-up costs. *Evasive:* only peak power or TDP.
5. **"Show me the voltage–frequency and performance–power curves."**
   *Strong:* full curves for both the new and the competing chip. *Evasive:* a single operating point chosen for the comparison.

### [14-02 · Instruction Set Architecture: RISC-V, Arm and x86](../../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-02-isa-risc-v-arm-x86.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"RISC-V is free."** *Reality:* the ISA licence is free; cores, verification, compilers, operating-system support and security certification are not. *Sanity check:* ask what the company pays for its cores, toolchain and verification, and how much of its software runs on RISC-V today.
- **"Our ISA makes our chip efficient."** *Reality:* the ISA sets decoding cost and instruction count, but process, microarchitecture, caches and design quality dominate efficiency. *Sanity check:* compare chips of the same process node and power class across ISAs.
- **"Licensing revenue is surging."** *Reality:* Arm's licence and other revenue rose from $1,839 M to $2,307 M in FY2026, but licence and other revenue from related parties rose from $418 M to $1,009 M, more than the whole increase [4]. *Sanity check:* read the related-party note before extrapolating licence growth to the market.
- **"Drop-in compatible."** *Reality:* compatibility is defined by the specification and its profiles; custom extensions and missing optional ones break binaries. *Sanity check:* ask which profile the chip conforms to, and whether it passes the official compatibility tests.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"Why this ISA, and what would it cost to move?"**
   *Strong:* a quantified comparison of licence costs, core performance, ecosystem readiness and switching cost. *Evasive:* "industry standard" with no numbers.
2. **"Which profile or architecture version do your cores implement, and how is compatibility verified?"**
   *Strong:* a named profile or version and the official test suites passed. *Evasive:* "fully compatible".
3. **"Which custom instructions have you added, and how does your software use them?"**
   *Strong:* specific extensions, compiler support and measured speedups on target workloads. *Evasive:* "proprietary acceleration".
4. **"What is your licence model and royalty exposure per unit?"**
   *Strong:* the licence type, royalty basis and how it scales with volume and price. *Evasive:* "standard terms".
5. **"How mature is the software ecosystem on this ISA for your market?"**
   *Strong:* named operating systems, toolchains, libraries and certifications available today. *Evasive:* "the community is growing fast".

### [14-03 · Assembly and the Compilation Stack](../../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-03-assembly-and-the-compilation-stack.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"2× faster with our new compiler."** *Reality:* such gains are usually on chosen kernels, sometimes from optimizations that only apply to the benchmark. *Sanity check:* ask for whole-application results, the flags used for both compilers, and whether the outputs were checked for correctness.
- **"Fully compatible: just recompile."** *Reality:* source compatibility (API) is not binary compatibility (ABI). Code that assumes `long` is 4 bytes, packs structures, uses inline assembly or relies on undefined behaviour breaks on a new target. *Sanity check:* ask how much of the customer's code base has actually been ported and tested.
- **"Our accelerator supports PyTorch."** *Reality:* "supports" may mean a subset of operators, with the rest falling back to the CPU. *Sanity check:* ask what fraction of the target models' operators run on the accelerator, measured end to end.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"Which compilers do you support, and is your backend upstream?"**
   *Strong:* named GCC and LLVM versions, patches merged upstream, and continuous testing against the upstream trunk. *Evasive:* "we have our own optimized compiler".
2. **"What is your ABI, and when did it last change?"**
   *Strong:* the standard psABI or a documented variant, with a versioning policy. *Evasive:* "it's standard" without specifics.
3. **"What fraction of your customers' code compiled and ran unchanged?"**
   *Strong:* a measured fraction across real code bases, with the categories of failures. *Evasive:* "everything we tried".
4. **"How do you benchmark compiler changes?"**
   *Strong:* a fixed suite of whole applications, with correctness checks and performance-regression tracking. *Evasive:* "we test on key kernels".
5. **"Who maintains your debugger, profiler and libraries?"**
   *Strong:* named teams or upstream projects, with release cadence. *Evasive:* "the community".

### [14-04 · Computer Arithmetic and Number Formats](../../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-04-computer-arithmetic-and-number-formats.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"FP4 with no accuracy loss."** *Reality:* accuracy depends on the model, the scaling scheme, which layers stay in higher precision, and whether the model was trained or fine-tuned for the format. *Sanity check:* ask for accuracy on the customer's model, against an FP16 or BF16 baseline, with the full quantization recipe.
- **"2× the TOPS of the competitor."** *Reality:* often FP4 or sparse figures against FP8 or dense ones. *Sanity check:* normalize to the same format, density and block scaling.
- **"Bit-exact with the GPU."** *Reality:* only if the accumulation order, accumulator width and rounding match. *Sanity check:* ask how reductions are ordered and whether results are deterministic across runs.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"How wide is your accumulator, and how often do you flush to FP32?"**
   *Strong:* the exact width and flush interval, and measured error against an FP32 reference. *Evasive:* "high precision".
2. **"Which scaling scheme do you support: per tensor, per channel, per block, and which block size?"**
   *Strong:* a list tied to the OCP MX specification and other formats, with accuracy data. *Evasive:* "full FP4 support".
3. **"Are your results deterministic run to run?"**
   *Strong:* yes in a defined mode, with its performance cost. *Evasive:* "within tolerance".
4. **"What happens on overflow and NaN in your low-precision paths?"**
   *Strong:* saturation or NaN behaviour per format, documented. *Evasive:* "it doesn't happen in practice".
5. **"How much accuracy do customers lose going from BF16 to FP8, and how much engineering does it take?"**
   *Strong:* measured numbers on named models, and the tooling that achieves them. *Evasive:* "negligible".

### [14-05 · Single-Cycle Datapath and Control](../../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-05-single-cycle-datapath.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"Single-cycle execution."** *Reality:* microcontroller vendors sometimes mean that *most instructions issue at one per clock*, not that a whole instruction completes within a single cycle as in this chapter; loads, branches and multiplies often take more. *Sanity check:* ask for the cycle counts per instruction class, including taken branches and memory stalls.
- **"Our core is fully RISC-V compliant."** *Reality:* compliance is per extension and per test suite; a small core may omit byte loads, CSRs or exceptions, as this chapter's does. *Sanity check:* ask which extensions are implemented and which official architectural tests pass.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"How do you verify that your core matches the ISA?"**
   *Strong:* lock-step comparison against a reference model (such as Sail or a vetted simulator), random instruction generation, and the official architectural tests, with coverage metrics. *Evasive:* "we run lots of software on it".
2. **"What sets your clock period?"**
   *Strong:* a named critical path (for example the data-cache access or the register-file read) with numbers, and what was done about it. *Evasive:* "the process node".
3. **"What is your cycle count for a taken branch, a load hit and a load miss?"**
   *Strong:* specific numbers per case. *Evasive:* "one instruction per cycle".
4. **"Which RISC-V extensions does the core implement, and which architectural tests does it pass?"**
   *Strong:* an explicit list, with test results. *Evasive:* "full RISC-V".

### [14-06 · Pipelining and Hazards](../../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-06-pipelining-and-hazards.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"Executes one instruction per cycle."** *Reality:* an ideal pipeline does; real code adds stalls and flushes. The lab's program, on a perfectly working five-stage core, runs at CPI 1.48. *Sanity check:* ask for measured CPI or IPC on the customer's code, not peak issue rate.
- **"Deeper pipeline, higher frequency, faster chip."** *Reality:* each extra stage raises the cost of every mispredicted branch and every load miss. *Sanity check:* compare performance per clock and performance per watt on real workloads, not frequency.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"What is your branch-misprediction penalty and your load-to-use latency, in cycles?"**
   *Strong:* specific numbers for both, and how they compare with competitors. *Evasive:* "industry-leading".
2. **"Where is your critical path, and how did you balance the stages?"**
   *Strong:* a named stage and path, and the trade made (for example, splitting cache access over two stages). *Evasive:* "we hit our frequency target".
3. **"What CPI do you measure on our workload, and how much of the loss is front end against back end?"**
   *Strong:* a top-down breakdown from performance counters. *Evasive:* a peak-IPC figure.
4. **"How do you verify the pipeline against the ISA?"**
   *Strong:* lock-step comparison with a reference model under random and directed tests, with coverage of hazard combinations. *Evasive:* "we boot Linux".

### [14-07 · Branch Prediction and Speculation](../../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-07-branch-prediction-and-speculation.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"99% branch prediction accuracy."** *Reality:* accuracy is workload-dependent and usually quoted on benchmark suites. *Sanity check:* ask for mispredictions per thousand instructions (MPKI) on the customer's workload, and for the misprediction penalty in cycles.
- **"Not affected by Spectre."** *Reality:* any processor that speculates past branches and has caches is, in principle, exposed to variant 1; what differs is how hard exploitation is and which mitigations are on by default. *Sanity check:* ask which CVE variants have been evaluated and which mitigations are enabled, with their measured cost.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"What are your misprediction penalty and MPKI on our workload?"**
   *Strong:* measured numbers from performance counters, with a breakdown by branch type. *Evasive:* a single accuracy percentage.
2. **"How do you isolate predictor state between security domains?"**
   *Strong:* specific mechanisms (flushing or partitioning on context switch, tagging by privilege level) and their cost. *Evasive:* "we follow industry guidance".
3. **"What do mitigations cost on our software stack?"**
   *Strong:* measured slowdowns with mitigations on and off, per workload. *Evasive:* "negligible".
4. **"How do you evaluate predictor changes?"**
   *Strong:* trace-driven and cycle-level simulation on large trace libraries, validated against silicon counters. *Evasive:* "on benchmarks".

### [14-08 · Out-of-Order and Superscalar Execution](../../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-08-out-of-order-and-superscalar.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"8-wide core."** *Reality:* the width is the maximum per cycle in one stage; sustained IPC on real code is usually far lower, limited by dependences, branches and cache misses. *Sanity check:* ask for measured IPC on representative workloads, and where the bottleneck is (front end, back end, memory).
- **"+16% IPC."** *Reality:* AMD's figure is an "up to" claim, the best result over its chosen benchmarks at fixed frequency; the average is lower. *Sanity check:* ask which benchmarks, and how the gain varies (memory-bound code may gain nothing).

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"What limits IPC on our workload: front end, execution or memory?"**
   *Strong:* a top-down breakdown from performance counters, with the dominant stall named. *Evasive:* a peak-width figure.
2. **"How large is your window, and what latency does it hide?"**
   *Strong:* ROB, scheduler and load/store-queue sizes, and the latencies they cover. *Evasive:* "industry-leading".
3. **"What did the last generation's IPC gain cost in area and power?"**
   *Strong:* specific numbers, and the trade-off reasoning. *Evasive:* "the new node paid for it".
4. **"How do you verify the out-of-order core?"**
   *Strong:* reference-model comparison at retirement, random tests, and formal checks of the rename and recovery logic. *Evasive:* "extensive simulation".

### [14-09 · Memory Hierarchy and Caches](../../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-09-memory-hierarchy-and-caches.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"Huge cache."** *Reality:* a larger cache helps only workloads whose working set fits in the new size but not the old one, and it raises hit latency. *Sanity check:* ask for the miss-rate or performance curve against cache size on your workload.
- **"X TB/s of memory bandwidth."** *Reality:* that is the pin rate times the width, a peak. Delivered bandwidth depends on access pattern, on enough outstanding requests, and on refresh and row overheads. *Sanity check:* ask for measured bandwidth on a streaming benchmark and on your access pattern.
- **"Up to N× faster with our new memory."** *Reality:* only memory-bound phases gain; compute-bound phases do not. *Sanity check:* ask what fraction of time the workload is memory-bound (a roofline, 14-15).

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"What is your workload's working set, and where does it sit in the hierarchy?"**
   *Strong:* miss rates or MPKI per level from counters, and the working-set curve. *Evasive:* "it fits in cache".
2. **"How much of your bandwidth is used, and what limits it?"**
   *Strong:* achieved against peak bandwidth, outstanding requests per core, and the effect of prefetchers. *Evasive:* the peak figure.
3. **"What did the last cache-size increase buy, and what did it cost in latency and area?"**
   *Strong:* specific performance per area, with the latency change. *Evasive:* "more is better".
4. **"How does the software stack exploit locality?"**
   *Strong:* tiled kernels, data-layout choices, prefetch hints, measured. *Evasive:* "the compiler handles it".

### [14-10 · Virtual Memory, TLBs and the OS Interface](../../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-10-virtual-memory.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"Unlimited memory."** *Reality:* virtual memory beyond physical memory means paging to storage, millions of cycles per fault. *Sanity check:* ask what happens to performance when the working set exceeds DRAM.
- **"Huge pages give X% speedup."** *Reality:* only TLB-bound workloads gain, and huge pages can waste memory and fragment physical memory. *Sanity check:* ask for the TLB-miss share of cycles before and after.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"How much time does your workload spend in TLB misses and page walks?"**
   *Strong:* a measured share from performance counters, and the page-size policy. *Evasive:* "the caches handle it".
2. **"How do you handle TLB shootdowns at your core counts?"**
   *Strong:* batching, ASIDs, and measured shootdown latency. *Evasive:* no data.
3. **"What is your worst-case interrupt latency?"**
   *Strong:* a bound with the conditions (disabled regions, pipeline drain). *Evasive:* a typical value only.
4. **"How is the kernel isolated from user code against speculative attacks?"**
   *Strong:* specific mitigations and their measured cost. *Evasive:* "we are not affected".

### [14-11 · I/O, Buses and Interconnect](../../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-11-io-buses-and-interconnect.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"X GB/s link."** *Reality:* often a bidirectional raw figure. *Sanity check:* ask for one-way delivered bandwidth after encoding, Flit and protocol overhead, at the packet sizes you use.
- **"Low-latency interrupts."** *Reality:* the hardware path is short, but software overhead dominates. *Sanity check:* ask for measured end-to-end latency and CPU cost per event at your event rate.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"Where is the bottleneck between the accelerator and its data?"**
   *Strong:* measured link utilization, transfer sizes, and overlap with compute. *Evasive:* the link's peak rate.
2. **"How many outstanding transactions do your fabric ports support, and at what latency?"**
   *Strong:* specific numbers, with the Little's-law bandwidth they imply. *Evasive:* "enough".
3. **"How is DMA kept coherent with the caches?"**
   *Strong:* hardware coherence, or a clear driver discipline with tests. *Evasive:* silence.
4. **"How do you verify interconnect protocol compliance?"**
   *Strong:* protocol checkers, formal properties for handshake rules, interoperability testing. *Evasive:* "it works in simulation".

### [14-12 · Multicore, Coherence and Memory Consistency](../../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-12-multicore-coherence-consistency.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"Linear scaling with cores."** *Reality:* true only for workloads with little sharing. *Sanity check:* ask for the scaling curve on a workload with shared state, and where it flattens.
- **"Coherent accelerator attach."** *Reality:* coherence makes sharing correct, not fast; fine-grained sharing across a link costs a link round trip per handoff. *Sanity check:* ask how often data actually moves between host and device caches.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"Where does coherence traffic limit your scaling?"**
   *Strong:* measured coherence misses or HITM-style counters per structure, and the fixes made. *Evasive:* "we use lock-free code".
2. **"How do you validate memory ordering on weakly ordered targets?"**
   *Strong:* litmus testing, model checking against the formal model, and stress tests on hardware. *Evasive:* "it passes on x86".
3. **"Snooping, directory or hybrid, and why at your core count?"**
   *Strong:* the trade-off in latency, bandwidth and storage, with numbers. *Evasive:* a product name.
4. **"How does your protocol behave under contention for one line?"**
   *Strong:* measured handoff latency and fairness. *Evasive:* only uncontended latency.

### [14-13 · GPUs and SIMT](../../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-13-gpus-and-simt.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"X PFLOPS."** *Reality:* usually sparse, at the narrowest format, at peak clock. *Sanity check:* ask for dense throughput at the precision your model uses, and measured utilization on your workload.
- **"Y TB/s of memory bandwidth."** *Reality:* achieved bandwidth on real kernels is lower, and many kernels are bandwidth-bound. *Sanity check:* ask for a roofline of key kernels.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"What utilization (MFU) do you reach on our model, at which precision?"**
   *Strong:* measured model-FLOPs utilization with the precision stated. *Evasive:* the peak figure.
2. **"Which kernels are memory-bound, and what is your plan for them?"**
   *Strong:* roofline placement, fusion and tiling plans. *Evasive:* "the next GPU is faster".
3. **"How do you handle divergence-heavy or sparse workloads?"**
   *Strong:* specific restructuring (binning, compaction), measured efficiency. *Evasive:* "the hardware handles it".
4. **"What does sparsity buy on our models in practice?"**
   *Strong:* accuracy and speed with 2:4 pruning, measured. *Evasive:* the doubled headline.

### [14-14 · AI Accelerators: Systolic Arrays, Dataflow and Low Precision](../../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-14-ai-accelerators.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"X POPS."** *Reality:* peak at the narrowest format, often with sparsity, at 100% utilization. *Sanity check:* ask for measured throughput on a named model at a stated precision and batch size.
- **"Up to N× faster than a GPU."** *Reality:* usually on one favourable benchmark. *Sanity check:* ask for a range of models, end-to-end including non-matrix operations and data loading.
- **"Lossless INT4."** *Reality:* accuracy depends on the model, calibration and scale granularity. *Sanity check:* ask for accuracy on your evaluation suite, against BF16.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"What utilization does your array reach on our layer shapes?"**
   *Strong:* measured per-layer utilization, including small and odd shapes. *Evasive:* peak only.
2. **"Where does your memory hierarchy put the weights and activations of our largest model?"**
   *Strong:* a placement plan with bandwidth per level. *Evasive:* "it fits in HBM".
3. **"What precision do you deploy, and what accuracy loss did you measure?"**
   *Strong:* numbers on named benchmarks, with calibration method. *Evasive:* "negligible".
4. **"How is decoding throughput limited on your chip?"**
   *Strong:* bandwidth-bound analysis, batching strategy, measured tokens/s at stated latency. *Evasive:* a TOPS figure.

### [14-15 · The Roofline Model, Benchmarks and How They Are Gamed](../../courses/14-computer-organization-and-architecture/chapters/14-15-roofline-and-benchmarks.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"N× faster."** *Reality:* on which benchmark, at which precision, which division, which batch size, and against which baseline? *Sanity check:* ask for the full table and the rules followed.
- **"Industry-leading SPEC score."** *Reality:* base or peak, and which suite version (2017 or 2026)? *Sanity check:* compare base results on the same suite.
- **"Record MLPerf result."** *Reality:* records are per benchmark, per scenario, per division and often per system size. *Sanity check:* find the matching result for the competitor in the same category.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. **"Where do our top five workloads sit on your roofline?"**
   *Strong:* measured intensities and achieved FLOPS, plotted. *Evasive:* peak TFLOPS.
2. **"Which benchmark results are base, Closed, dense and sustained?"**
   *Strong:* each qualifier answered. *Evasive:* "industry standard".
3. **"What is your performance per watt and per dollar on our workload?"**
   *Strong:* measured, with the power and price basis. *Evasive:* performance alone.
4. **"How did you choose the workloads you report?"**
   *Strong:* a stated selection rule, with losses shown. *Evasive:* only wins.

## [19 · Digital VLSI Design](../../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/README.md)

### [19-01 · The CMOS Inverter: Static Characteristics](../../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-01-cmos-inverter-static.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"Operates down to X mV."** A ring oscillator or an inverter chain working at a very low supply in a lab is not a product. Ask at what temperature and process corner, with what yield, at what speed, and whether memories and I/O run at the same supply.
- **"Symmetric" or "balanced" cells.** Rise and fall delays can be balanced at one corner; across temperature and process they drift apart, because the NMOS and PMOS respond differently.
- **Noise-margin claims.** A static margin from a unity-gain point says little about dynamic noise (supply bounce, crosstalk, 19-05). Ask how the design was signed off for noise.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. *"What is your lowest functional supply, and what sets it: logic, SRAM or timing?"* Strong: SRAM usually limits first (19-08), with data across corners and a plan (assist circuits, separate rails). Evasive: a single lab number without corners.
2. *"How do your libraries choose PMOS sizing?"* Strong: optimized for delay and area per cell, with the noise-margin consequences characterized. Evasive: "we use the foundry defaults" without knowing their tradeoffs.
3. *"How much voltage margin do you carry for variation, and how do you measure it on silicon?"* Strong: a budget split into process, voltage, temperature and aging, verified with on-chip monitors and adaptive voltage scaling. Evasive: "a standard 10%".
4. *"What happens to your design at the slow-cold corner at minimum supply?"* Strong: specific timing and noise numbers, and the yield impact. Evasive: "it's covered by signoff".

### [19-02 · The CMOS Inverter: Dynamic Behavior and Delay](../../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-02-cmos-inverter-dynamic.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"X% faster" at a new node.** Ask at what supply, threshold flavor and load: an inverter-only ring oscillator, an FO4 chain and a real critical path with wires and memories improve by different amounts.
- **"Up to N GHz."** A clock frequency claim is meaningful only with its voltage and temperature; ask for the voltage–frequency curve.
- **"15% faster or 30% less power".** The two are alternatives, not a sum: §3.7's delay–supply curve lets a faster transistor be spent as speed at the same supply or as a lower supply at the same speed. Ask which one the product uses, and at what point on the curve.
- **Ring-oscillator speed-ups.** A ring has almost no wire load, so it flatters a process whose transistors improved more than its interconnect (19-05).

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. *"How many FO4 delays fit in your clock period, and how does that compare with your competitors?"* Strong: a number (and how much of it is flip-flop and clock overhead, 19-07), with the reasoning behind the pipeline depth. Evasive: only GHz figures.
2. *"Where does your critical path's delay go: gates, wires or memories?"* Strong: a breakdown from timing reports, with the plan for each part. Evasive: "we'll fix it with a faster process".
3. *"What is your voltage–frequency curve at the low end, and what limits it?"* Strong: measured data across corners and what sets the minimum (often SRAM, 19-08). Evasive: one operating point.
4. *"How do your library cells' delays depend on input slope, and how do you keep slopes in check?"* Strong: maximum-transition constraints and buffering, with characterized tables. Evasive: "the tools handle it".

### [19-03 · Combinational Logic Families](../../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-03-logic-families.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"Custom-designed for speed."** Ask which blocks are custom (dynamic or hand-sized) and which are synthesized; custom blocks are fast but harder to port to the next node, which matters for a roadmap.
- **"Fewer transistors."** Pass-transistor and dynamic styles save transistors per gate, but buffers, keepers, level restorers and clock loads can give back much of the saving; compare whole blocks, not gates.
- **Gate counts.** A "gate" in marketing material usually means a NAND2-equivalent area unit, not a logic gate; ask for the unit before comparing.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. *"Which parts of your design use anything other than static CMOS standard cells, and why?"* Strong: a short list (register files, specific datapaths) with the speed or area gain measured. Evasive: "we use whatever is fastest".
2. *"How do you verify dynamic nodes for charge sharing, leakage and noise across corners?"* Strong: dedicated noise-analysis tools and margins, with silicon correlation. Evasive: "timing signoff covers it".
3. *"What limits the fan-in of your library's gates, and how does synthesis choose between a wide gate and a tree?"* Strong: characterized delay tables and logical-effort reasoning. Evasive: no answer beyond "the tools decide".
4. *"How portable are your custom circuits to the next node?"* Strong: a plan and an estimate of the redesign effort. Evasive: an assumption that they port automatically.

### [19-04 · Transistor Sizing and Logical Effort](../../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-04-sizing-and-logical-effort.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"Our design runs at N GHz."** Ask how many FO4 delays fit in the cycle and how much of it is sequencing overhead (19-07). A higher frequency can come from a faster process, from deeper pipelining, or from aggressive sizing, with very different costs.
- **"Optimized for speed."** Minimum-delay sizing costs disproportionate area and power for the last few percent; ask where on the delay–area curve the design sits.
- **Gate-delay claims from simple chains.** Inverter chains are the best case; real paths have branching, wide gates and wires.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. *"How many FO4 delays are in your critical path, and how much margin do you keep?"* Strong: a number with a breakdown into logic, wire and sequencing overhead. Evasive: only a frequency.
2. *"How do you decide between deeper pipelining and faster logic?"* Strong: a quantified tradeoff of FO4 per stage, flip-flop overhead and power. Evasive: "we follow the previous generation".
3. *"Where does your design spend area on upsizing, and what would relaxing the clock by 10% save?"* Strong: data from synthesis sweeps. Evasive: no data.
4. *"How are high-fan-out nets (clocks, resets, enables) buffered?"* Strong: dedicated trees with controlled stage effort and slopes. Evasive: "the tools handle it".

### [19-05 · Interconnect](../../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-05-interconnect.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"X% faster transistors."** Paths dominated by wires improve much less; ask for the improvement on a representative critical path with its wiring, not on a ring oscillator.
- **"Backside power gives Y% more performance."** The gain comes mainly from lower IR drop and freed routing, and depends heavily on the design; ask what design it was measured on and at what utilization.
- **Density claims.** A smaller cell is only usable if the wires can route it; ask about achieved utilization, not just cell area.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. *"How far can a signal travel in one clock cycle in your design, and how did that shape your floorplan?"* Strong: a number in millimetres with the repeater strategy. Evasive: "we close timing".
2. *"What share of your dynamic power is in wires and clock?"* Strong: a measured or estimated split, and the actions taken. Evasive: only a total.
3. *"How do you handle crosstalk in signoff?"* Strong: coupling-aware timing, noise analysis and shielding rules for critical nets. Evasive: "we add margin".
4. *"What does backside power delivery buy you on your design, and at what cost?"* Strong: specific IR-drop and utilization results and the cost and thermal implications. Evasive: the foundry's headline number.

### [19-06 · Power and Low-Power Design](../../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-06-power-and-low-power-design.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"X% lower power."** Ask: at what frequency, voltage, temperature and workload; dynamic or leakage; and compared with what. Power at a fixed frequency and energy per task can move in opposite directions.
- **"Near-threshold" or "subthreshold" claims.** Ask what runs at that voltage (logic, SRAM, I/O?), at what speed and temperature, and with what yield (19-01, 19-08).
- **TDP.** Thermal design power is a cooling specification, not a measurement of typical or peak electrical power.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. *"What fraction of your power is dynamic, leakage and clock, in active use and in standby?"* Strong: a breakdown by block from measured silicon. Evasive: one total number.
2. *"How many voltage–frequency operating points do you use, and how fast can you switch between them?"* Strong: specific points, transition times and the governor policy. Evasive: "we support DVFS".
3. *"Which blocks are power-gated, and what are their wake-up times and break-even times?"* Strong: a table. Evasive: "everything is power-gated".
4. *"What is your leakage at the hot, fast corner, and how does it constrain your thermal design?"* Strong: numbers and the guard-band strategy. Evasive: typical-corner numbers only.

### [19-07 · Sequential Circuits, Timing and Clocking](../../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-07-sequential-timing-and-clocking.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"Higher frequency."** Ask whether it comes from deeper pipelining (more overhead and latency per instruction) or from faster logic; instructions per cycle may fall.
- **"Zero-skew clock tree."** Nominal skew can be zero; variation, temperature gradients and supply noise are not. Ask for the skew and jitter budget at signoff.
- **"Metastability-free."** No synchronous capture of an asynchronous signal is free of metastability; ask for the MTBF calculation and its assumptions.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. *"What is your cycle time in FO4, and how much of it is sequencing overhead and clock uncertainty?"* Strong: a breakdown. Evasive: only gigahertz.
2. *"How do you close hold timing across corners, and how many hold buffers does the design carry?"* Strong: corner strategy and buffer counts. Evasive: "the tool fixes hold".
3. *"How do you verify clock-domain crossings?"* Strong: structural CDC analysis plus MTBF targets per crossing. Evasive: "we use two flops".
4. *"What fraction of your power is the clock network, and how much does gating save?"* Strong: measured numbers. Evasive: no breakdown.

### [19-08 · SRAM Design](../../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-08-sram-design.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"Densest SRAM cell."** Cell area is not macro density; ask for the density of a usable macro with periphery, at what supply and speed.
- **"Operates down to X V."** Ask whether the SRAM runs at that voltage, or on a separate higher rail, and with what assists.
- **"Same cache at lower cost."** If the SRAM cell did not shrink between nodes, a cache-heavy design may not get cheaper.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. *"What is your SRAM's $V_{min}$, and is it above your logic's?"* Strong: measured distributions across corners, with the assist and rail strategy. Evasive: a single typical number.
2. *"How much redundancy and ECC do your memories carry, and what repair rate do you see in production?"* Strong: numbers and trends. Evasive: "yield is fine".
3. *"How does your cache area scale at the next node?"* Strong: a cell- and macro-level comparison. Evasive: the logic-density headline only.
4. *"Do you use 6T or 8T cells for register files, and why?"* Strong: port counts, stability and area tradeoffs. Evasive: no answer.

### [19-09 · Layout, Design Rules and Standard Cells](../../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-09-layout-and-standard-cells.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"X MTr/mm² density."** Peak transistor density comes from the densest cells in ideal conditions; real designs mix cells, SRAM and analog and run below full utilization.
- **"Smaller cell height."** Ask what drive strength and routing the shorter cells keep, and what utilization real designs achieve with them.
- **"DRC-clean layout."** Clean against which rule deck, at which version, and with which waivers?

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. *"What utilization do your blocks achieve, and what limits it?"* Strong: numbers per block, with congestion and timing as the stated limits. Evasive: a single target.
2. *"Which library heights and threshold flavors do you use, and why?"* Strong: a reasoned mix tied to performance and leakage targets. Evasive: "the foundry default".
3. *"How do you manage DRC and LVS closure late in a project?"* Strong: incremental signoff and tracked waivers. Evasive: "we fix them at the end".
4. *"How much of your design is custom layout, and how portable is it?"* Strong: specific blocks with porting plans. Evasive: no inventory.

### [19-10 · The ASIC Flow I: Synthesis and Static Timing Analysis](../../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-10-synthesis-and-sta.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"AI improves PPA by 10–25 %."** The vendors' own figures: Synopsys DSO.ai customers saw "more than 3x productivity increases, up to 25% lower total power" (2023) and "a more than 10% boost in performance, power, area (PPA), up to 10X faster turn-around time" against optimization without AI (2024); Cadence Cerebrus offered productivity "up to 10X versus a manual approach" and "up to a 20% better" PPA (2021), with customers reporting 8 % power on critical blocks (Samsung), 5 % area and 6 % power (MediaTek) and a 75 % improvement in total negative slack (Renesas) ([R-318]). **[Vendor claim]** for all of them. Ask for the baseline (an expert team with the same compute, or a default flow?), the block types, and whether the result was signed off at every corner; a 75 % TNS improvement does not say the design closed. These tools search flow settings (synthesis and placement options, constraints, effort levels) automatically. I found no independent benchmark of either vendor's numbers.
- **"Golden signoff."** It means the foundry, the IP vendors and customers accept the tool's results, which is commercially decisive; it does not mean the results are physical truth. Every number still comes from characterized Liberty tables and extracted parasitics, and silicon correlation is a separate claim to ask for.
- **"Timing is closed."** Ask at which corners and modes, with what uncertainty and derates, with how many exceptions, and after which stage (synthesis, placement or post-route). A design "closed" at the typical corner with zero uncertainty, like the open flow's defaults, has not been signed off.
- **"Runs at X GHz on node Y."** Frequency depends on the corner and the margins assumed. The open flow's 1.1 ns `gcd` on SKY130 is a regression target on a tiny design, not a statement about the process.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. *"What is your worst negative slack and total negative slack at each signoff corner today, and how has it trended over the last month?"* Strong: numbers per scenario and a trend. Evasive: "timing is basically closed".
2. *"How many timing exceptions are in your constraints, and who reviews them?"* Strong: a count, a reason for each, and a review process. Evasive: no count.
3. *"What clock uncertainty and OCV model do you use at signoff, and where do the numbers come from?"* Strong: foundry-recommended LVF/POCV with stated sigma, uncertainty broken into jitter and margin. Evasive: "the default".
4. *"How much did slack change between synthesis and post-route signoff?"* Strong: a measured correlation and the margin they reserve for it. Evasive: surprise at the question.
5. *"How many mode-corner scenarios do you sign off, and which ones limit setup and hold?"* Strong: a scenario matrix with the dominant corners named. Evasive: one corner.

### [19-11 · The ASIC Flow II: Floorplan, Place and Route, Signoff](../../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-11-place-route-signoff.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"10 to 20 percent better PPA" from a new tool.** Ask: compared with which tool and version, on which designs, with what effort from expert users of each? A flow tuned by its vendor on chosen blocks is not a controlled experiment, and gains rarely add up across successive releases.
- **"Taped out with open-source tools."** True for hundreds of SKY130 and GF180 designs; ask which signoff checks were run (DRC, LVS, timing at which corners), whether the chip worked, and what was hand-fixed. Open-flow regression targets have tolerated negative slack.
- **"Our design closed at X GHz."** At which corner, with what utilization and with what clock uncertainty and derates (19-10)? A block closed at 35 % utilization with optimistic margins is a different product from one closed at 70 % with signoff margins.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. *"What utilization did your blocks close at, and how much area went to buffers inserted after placement?"* Strong: per-block numbers and trend across tape-outs. Evasive: "it routes".
2. *"What is your worst static and dynamic IR drop, and what voltage does timing signoff assume?"* Strong: drop maps and a stated budget used consistently. Evasive: IR drop treated only as a reliability check.
3. *"How did slack change from placement to post-route signoff, and how many timing-closure iterations did the last tape-out take?"* Strong: measured correlation and a planned margin. Evasive: surprises close to tape-out.
4. *"Which signoff tools do you trust, and are any of them the same code as your implementation tools?"* Strong: independent, foundry-qualified signoff. Evasive: the implementation tool's own reports.
5. *"For an open-source flow: which checks ran at signoff and what did silicon show?"* Strong: DRC/LVS clean, multi-corner timing, measured results. Evasive: "it passed the flow".

### [19-12 · Design for Test: Scan, BIST and ATPG](../../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-12-design-for-test.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"400X compression."** Ask what the baseline is (uncompressed scan or the vendor's previous compression), how many extra patterns the compressed flow needs, and what the test-time reduction is. The same 2016 release that claimed compression "beyond 400X" claimed "up to 3X" less test time, and ITRS cautioned that pattern compression "does little to help reduce test times": the shift-time saving is bounded by the chain ratio, and the fixed per-die steps of §3.4 remain.
- **"99 % fault coverage."** Of which fault model, and of detectable faults only? At 80 % yield, 99 % stuck-at coverage still implies about 2200 DPPM by Williams–Brown; real quality depends on transition, cell-aware and memory coverage too.
- **"Zero defects."** A target, not a measurement. Ask for field-return data in DPPM over a stated volume and period.
- **"Fully tested at the factory."** The hyperscaler studies show that some defects escape or appear later; ask what in-field self-test and screening the product supports.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. *"Which fault models do you test in production (stuck-at, transition, cell-aware, memory), with what coverage, and what DPPM do you see in the field?"* Strong: per-model numbers and field data. Evasive: "over 99 % coverage".
2. *"What is your test time per die, how many sites in parallel, and what compression ratio and pattern inflation do you get?"* Strong: measured numbers and a cost model. Evasive: the vendor's datasheet ratio.
3. *"For automotive parts: what are your single-point and latent-fault metrics, and how are latent faults detected in the field?"* Strong: metrics per ASIL with BIST coverage figures. Evasive: "we are ISO 26262 certified".
4. *"For datacenter parts: what in-field test hooks do you expose for fleet screening, and how do you handle a mercurial core?"* Strong: documented self-test, telemetry and core isolation. Evasive: "our manufacturing test is thorough".
5. *"How do test failures feed back into yield learning?"* Strong: volume diagnosis tied to layout and process data. Evasive: failing dies are just discarded.

### [19-13 · Verification: Simulation, UVM, Formal and Emulation](../../courses/19-digital-vlsi-design/chapters/19-13-verification-methods.md)

**Marketing vs Reality.**

- **"100 % coverage."** Of which model, code or functional, with how many waived bins? Coverage measures stimulus, not checking.
- **"Formally verified."** Which properties, under which assumptions, on which blocks, and were the proofs full or bounded? A whole SoC is never formally verified end to end.
- **"First-silicon success."** Functional only, or also performance and yield? Did a metal-layer fix count as a spin?
- **"48 billion gates of capacity."** Capacity is not speed or turnaround: ask for run speed on your design, compile time and debug visibility.

**Questions for engineering leaders.**

1. *"How many spins did your last three chips need, and what was the root cause of each?"* Strong: per-spin causes and what changed in the flow. Evasive: "we're usually first-pass".
2. *"How is your verification plan tied to coverage, and what closure numbers and waivers did you sign off with?"* Strong: plan-linked functional coverage with reviewed waivers. Evasive: "100 % code coverage".
3. *"Which blocks are formally proven, and are the proofs full or bounded?"* Strong: named blocks, properties and assumptions with their review. Evasive: "we use formal".
4. *"When did software first run on the RTL, on what platform?"* Strong: emulation or prototypes months before tape-out. Evasive: "software starts on silicon".
5. *"What did your bug-discovery curve look like in the last ten weeks before tape-out?"* Strong: a flattening curve at steady regression volume. Evasive: a date-driven signoff.
